Reproductive output in Common lynceus (Lynceus brachyurus) is highly variable, but continuous rearing at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] provides a stable framework for estimating key rates. Under these controlled thermal conditions, females begin producing clutches quite early, with the time since birth at puberty measured at approximately 11 days [tp = approximately 11 days] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This rapid maturation allows for a prolonged adult phase. Individual females carry broods of varying size, but at their reproductive peak they have been observed to deposit around 80 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = around 80 eggs per clutch], with a new clutch being produced approximately every half day, translating to about two clutches per day [F_R_i = about two clutches per day]. This high-frequency, moderate-fecundity strategy underpins the species' maximum reproductive rate. The carapace length at which this pubertal transition occurs is relatively small, measuring only 0.3 cm [Lp = 0.3 cm], and the corresponding carapace width at that same developmental stage is 2.5 mm. Adults that have completed their somatic growth reach a more substantial size, with an ultimate carapace length of 0.7 cm [Li = 0.7 cm].

The wet weight at birth for newly hatched juveniles is exceedingly low, calculated at 0.0000045 grams [Wwb = 0.0000045 grams]. This near-microscopic initial mass, derived from an egg diameter approximating 205 micrometres, places the neonate among the smallest free-living stages in the branchiopod lineage. The mass gain required to reach the adult stage is therefore dramatic, increasing by several orders of magnitude. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual, which exhibits a robust body shape roughly 0.6 cm in height and 0.6 cm in thickness, is approximately 0.099 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.099 grams]. This substantial increase in biomass, from a few micrograms to nearly one-tenth of a gram, is achieved through efficient filter feeding on suspended particles in temporary freshwater habitats. The contrast between the minute birth mass and the relatively large adult mass highlights the profound developmental investment required during the juvenile growth phase.

Under optimal laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the lifespan of Common lynceus has been documented to extend to 150 days [am = 150 days]. This longevity, spanning over five months in a controlled setting, is noteworthy for such a small crustacean and likely reflects the absence of predation and stable food resources provided in the lab. In natural temporary ponds, however, the realized lifespan is often curtailed by habitat desiccation, resulting in a much shorter duration. The complete life cycle, from hatching through pubertal development to eventual senescence, is thus tightly compressed within a single wet season for many wild populations. The maximum reproductive capacity observed at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] underscores the species' ability to rapidly colonize ephemeral waters, producing a substantial number of resting eggs that persist through dry periods.

Lynceus brachyurus exhibits a striking allometric relationship between its linear dimensions and its mass. The carapace, which encloses the entire body, grows to a maximum length of 0.7 cm [Li = 0.7 cm] in reproductively active adults, while the body itself reaches a volumetric fullness reflected in the 0.099 grams [Wwi = 0.099 grams] measure. Animals that are just reaching reproductive competence, identifiable by a carapace length of 0.3 cm [Lp = 0.3 cm] and a width of 2.5 mm, are considerably lighter but have already undergone a tremendous relative mass gain from the birth stage. The 0.0000045 grams [Wwb = 0.0000045 grams] neonate must increase its mass over 20,000-fold to approach the adult value. This trajectory is typical of organisms that hatch from small, nutrient-rich eggs and then exploit abundant microbial and algal blooms in their transient habitat, channeling nearly all assimilated energy into somatic growth during the first week of life before the pubertal carapace length is attained.

The ovigerous adult phase in Lynceus brachyurus is characterized by intense reproductive activity. Females continuously produce clutches, with a maximum observed output of 80 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 80 eggs per clutch] and a clutch frequency of approximately two clutches per day [F_R_i = approximately two clutches per day] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This combination yields a substantial daily reproductive potential, although actual fecundity varies widely depending on nutritional conditions. The onset of this prolific stage occurs at roughly 11 days [tp = roughly 11 days] after hatching, following a brief juvenile period. at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]The species' ultimate carapace length of 0.7 cm [Li = 0.7 cm] provides the body cavity necessary to accommodate the developing eggs. Following the peak reproductive period, individuals continue to reproduce until their natural death, which under constant temperature conditions occurs after a maximum lifespan of 150 days [am = 150 days] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The persistence of this species in unpredictable environments is a direct consequence of this rapid, high-output life history.
